description_en: The monument is situated on a terrace along the left bank of the Pādukā River (Pādukā Khola), a few meters to the south-east of the Pādukāsthān Jvālā Mandira (DLK0270).Pādukāsthān is a part of the Pañcakośī area, which attracts pilgrims from all over western Nepal. These sites are famous for their flame temples, where natural gas flames are believed to mark the spots where the body parts of Satī, an ancient Hindu goddess, fell when Lord Śiva carried her charred body (Lecomte-Tilouine 2009). Pādukāsthān specifically marks the place where Satī's feet (pādukā) fell.The Dhunighar is a two-storied, freestanding monument constructed with stone and mud masonry. It faces east and has a veranda consisting of three bays adorned with intricately carved wooden pillars. The space behind the veranda is used by the priests for performing certain rituals. Adjacent to a small pit containing ashes from thedhunifire, there is a priest's seat adorned with medieval sculptures. This area leads to two separate rooms. The southernmost room houses the sacreddhunifire. The roof is covered with tiles and supported by uncarved wooden struts.In addition to its religious significance, the building also serves as a shelter for pilgrims.According to local sources, the monument was originally constructed around 150 years ago, during the mid-19th century. It underwent renovation in 2015.
monument_assessment: Restored, Good (very few light surface damages, renovated or repaired)
references: REFERENCES Lecomte-Tilouine, Marie. 2009, “The Panchakoshi of Dullu. The Fire Frame of the Malla Imperial Capital”, in Bards and Mediums. History, Culture and Politics in the Central Himalayan Kingdoms , Marie Lecomte-Tilouine (ed.). Almora: Almora Book Depot, pp. 253-276.
